text: Every ninety minutes, a satellite circles our planet, capturing more data than it can ever send home.
So what if it could think for itself?
Star eye-cue. Intelligence, in orbit.
With AI on board, a satellite sends answers, not raw data, and reacts without waiting for Earth.
But space is hostile to computers.
One radiation particle can change data inside an AI chip.
Linux can crash.
Or worse, the system keeps running, while its answer is silently wrong.
Our research, published in I triple E and on NASA's website, is the first comparison of radiation-sensitive Linux components across three commercial chip platforms.
The newest platform ran two to three times longer. That evidence shows us which software to protect.
Star eye-cue combines hardened Linux, AI protection, and automatic recovery, in one platform.
It keeps the operating system alive, catches corrupted AI results, restores the workload, and recovers on its own, with no operator on Earth.
And the shift to orbital AI has already begun.
Google launched a prototype AI satellite.
Starcloud flew Nvidia's H one hundred in orbit.
SpaceX has proposed up to a million orbital data-center satellites.
All in a space economy heading past one trillion dollars.
We'll sell protected AI compute modules and software licences, and fly Satellite Zero, our own pilot mission, starting with Earth observation, disaster monitoring, and communications.
Star eye-cue is led by Doctor Saad Memon, a PhD in radiation-resilient computing, with co-founders from NASA and the European Space Agency.
We're raising one point five million euros, to go from prototype, to radiation validation and customer pilots, to an orbital demonstration, in twenty-four months.
Star eye-cue. Powerful AI, built for space.
